# Czech artist sparks EU row with provocative ‘Entropa’ installation

**BRUSSELS, Belgium** — A massive artwork commissioned to mark the Czech Republic’s presidency of the European Union has triggered controversy across the bloc, after member states were depicted through a series of provocative national stereotypes.

“Entropa,” created by Czech sculptor David Černý and installed at the European Council building in Brussels in January 2009, presents Europe as a giant model kit, with each EU country represented by a satirical image.

Bulgaria was shown as a network of Turkish-style squat toilets — a depiction the Bulgarian government condemned as insulting and humiliating.

Officials in Sofia submitted a formal protest and demanded that the section be removed. The image was subsequently covered with black fabric.

“We cannot accept the portrayal of our country in this way,” Bulgarian officials said at the time, arguing that the work crossed the line from satire into offense.

Other member states also received an irreverent treatment. Germany was represented by a web of highways that some observers said resembled a swastika. The Netherlands appeared submerged beneath water, with only mosque minarets visible. France was covered by a banner declaring “On Strike,” while Italy was portrayed as a football pitch.

Romania became a Dracula-themed amusement park, Denmark was assembled from Lego-like bricks, and Sweden was depicted as a flat-pack furniture box. The United Kingdom — known for its strained relationship with European integration — was missing from the map altogether.

The controversy deepened when Černý admitted that the project had not been created by 27 artists from across the EU, as initially claimed. The artist said he and a small group of Czech collaborators had produced the entire installation, inventing names and biographies for the supposed national contributors.

Černý apologized for misleading officials but defended the deception as part of the artwork.

“We knew the truth would come out,” he said in a statement. “But before that, we wanted to find out if Europe is able to laugh at itself.”

The Czech government, which had commissioned the piece, said it had believed the installation was a genuine collaboration involving artists from every member state. Czech officials apologized to countries that felt offended but initially resisted calls to dismantle the work, emphasizing the importance of artistic freedom.

Černý, one of the Czech Republic’s best-known contemporary artists, has built a career around politically charged and deliberately confrontational works. His sculptures have frequently mocked authority, nationalism and public institutions.

“Entropa” was intended to highlight the clichés Europeans hold about one another. Instead, it became a test of where the EU draws the line between political satire and national insult.

For Bulgaria, that line was clear. Its toilet-shaped representation remained concealed, while the rest of the installation stayed on display — leaving visitors to decide whether the work exposed Europe’s prejudices or merely repeated them.

# Czech Government Duped by Artist Behind Provocative EU Installation

**BRUSSELS —** The Czech government has acknowledged that artist David Černý fabricated the identities of 27 European artists supposedly involved in *Entropa*, a monumental installation commissioned to mark the Czech Republic’s 2009 presidency of the European Union.

The work, unveiled at the European Council’s Justus Lipsius building in Brussels, depicts the EU’s member states through exaggerated national stereotypes. Czech officials had presented it as a collaboration in which one artist from each of the bloc’s 27 countries interpreted his or her homeland. In reality, Černý created the installation with a small group of Czech associates and invented names, biographies and websites for the purported contributors.

Deputy Prime Minister Alexandr Vondra, who was responsible for European affairs, said he had learned only shortly before the public unveiling that Černý had not fulfilled the terms of the commission.

“I was unpleasantly surprised to learn that the creator of *Entropa*, David Černý, did not meet his commitment,” Vondra said in a statement. He added that the Czech government had believed the project involved artists from all 27 EU countries and that Černý bore responsibility for the deception.

Černý admitted the fabrication and apologized to the government, while arguing that the hoax was part of the artwork’s purpose.

“We knew the truth would come out,” he said. “But before that we wanted to find out if Europe is able to laugh at itself.”

## A Union Built From Stereotypes

*Entropa* resembles a giant plastic model kit, with each member state represented as a detachable component. The depictions range from playful to openly insulting.

Bulgaria is shown as a series of squat toilets. The Netherlands appears almost entirely submerged beneath water, with only mosque minarets visible. Romania is represented by a Dracula-themed amusement park, while Denmark is assembled from Lego-like bricks. Italy becomes a football pitch populated by players making suggestive gestures, and Luxembourg is displayed as a small object marked “For Sale.”

Germany’s section consists of a network of motorways that some observers said resembled a swastika, although Černý denied that interpretation. Britain is absent from the installation altogether—a joke about the country’s traditionally uneasy relationship with European integration.

The sharpest official protest came from Bulgaria. Bulgarian representatives described the toilet imagery as offensive and demanded that the section be removed. Bulgaria’s ambassador to the EU, Boyko Kotzev, called the portrayal “a humiliation for the Bulgarian nation and an offence to national dignity.”

Czech officials initially defended the installation as an exercise in irony and free expression. The discovery that the multinational collaboration had been fabricated, however, turned what had been intended as a provocative cultural opening for the Czech presidency into a diplomatic embarrassment.

Vondra said the government would consider its response while seeking to preserve freedom of artistic expression. A curtain was later placed over the Bulgarian section at Sofia’s request.

## A Career Built on Provocation

The controversy was consistent with Černý’s long record of public stunts and politically charged sculpture.

He first gained international attention in 1991, when he and several friends painted a Soviet tank monument in Prague bright pink. The tank had commemorated the Red Army’s arrival in the city at the end of the Second World War, but for many Czechs it had also come to symbolize decades of Soviet domination. Černý was briefly arrested, and the incident became an early post-communist confrontation over who controlled public memory.

Among his best-known later works are the enormous faceless infants crawling up Prague’s Žižkov Television Tower. Similar bronze “Babies” have appeared on Kampa Island, their faces replaced by barcode-like depressions.

His sculpture *Piss* places two male figures in a pool shaped like the Czech Republic. The figures move their hips and direct streams of water into the basin, spelling out quotations—or messages sent by visitors.

Another work, *Shark*, presented a lifelike figure of Saddam Hussein suspended in a tank of formaldehyde, parodying Damien Hirst’s famous preserved shark. Černý has also produced *Hanging Man*, a sculpture of Sigmund Freud dangling by one hand from a pole high above a street, alarming passers-by who have sometimes mistaken it for a suicide attempt.

That history made Černý an obvious choice for a Czech presidency that adopted the slogan “Europe Without Barriers” and sought to project an irreverent image. But officials said the commission had depended on the project being genuinely European.

The artist’s deception may ultimately reinforce *Entropa*’s central theme: that Europe’s national identities are shaped not only by how countries see themselves, but by the caricatures imposed on them by their neighbors. For the Czech government, however, the revelation left a less abstract question—how an official EU presidency project, complete with fictional artists and fabricated credentials, passed without adequate scrutiny.

- **Bulgaria** depicted as a collection of interconnected squat—or “Turkish”—toilets

Černý initially claimed that artists from all 27 member states had designed their own sections, but later admitted that he and a small group of collaborators had created nearly all of it.

Bulgaria summoned the Czech ambassador because its toilet depiction was regarded as humiliating and offensive, especially given the label “Turkish toilets” and Bulgaria’s historical sensitivities concerning Ottoman rule. The Bulgarian government formally protested, and the Bulgarian portion of the installation was subsequently covered with black cloth.
